lesson.overview: Build a physical standby database for Oracle Database 19c and understand every stage: prerequisites, primary preparation, duplicate/restore strategy, redo transport, redo apply, and operational validation. This chapter is a guided reference for an isolated lab. It is not a production change script.

sections.heading: 1. What a physical standby is — and what it protects

blocks.text: A physical standby is a second database maintained as a block-for-block physical replica of the primary. Oracle keeps it synchronized by shipping redo generated on the primary and applying that redo on the standby. The standby has the same DBID as the primary, while DB_UNIQUE_NAME distinguishes the database members in the Data Guard configuration.

The key idea is that Data Guard does not continuously copy changed datafiles over the network. It transports redo: the record of database changes. The standby uses recovery to reproduce those changes in the same order. This is why redo transport health and redo apply health must be monitored separately.

blocks.label: Remember
blocks.text: Redo transport answers: “Did the redo reach the standby?” Redo apply answers: “Has the standby applied the redo?” A healthy transport path does not automatically prove that apply is keeping up.
Business purpose

items: Disaster recovery: maintain a recoverable copy at another failure domain or site.
Planned maintenance: support a controlled switchover when the standby is ready and the change plan permits it.
Availability architecture: reduce recovery time compared with rebuilding a database after a major outage.
Read-only reporting is a separate design consideration; opening a physical standby for real-time query requires the appropriate Active Data Guard capability and licensing review.

blocks.text: A standby is not a substitute for independent backups. Logical corruption, accidental deletes, compromised credentials, or replicated bad changes can also reach the standby. Retain tested backups and recovery procedures.

sections.heading: 2. Architecture — follow one change from primary to standby

blocks.text: A user commits a transaction on the primary. Oracle records the change in redo. Data Guard transport processes send redo to the remote destination. The standby receives it through the remote file server (RFS), writes it to standby redo logs when configured for real-time transport, and the managed recovery process (MRP) applies the redo to the standby datafiles.
Components and responsibilities

rows: Primary database
Generates redo for committed and relevant database changes.
ARCHIVELOG mode, FORCE LOGGING policy, role, unique name and destination configuration.
LNS / transport
Moves redo from the primary to the remote destination (implementation varies by transport mode and release).
Destination status, network path, transport errors and redo throughput.
RFS
Receives redo on the standby and writes incoming redo to standby redo logs or archived redo logs.
RFS processes, standby redo log configuration and alert log.
Standby redo logs (SRLs)
Provide landing files for incoming redo and enable real-time apply when configured appropriately.
Thread coverage, group count, size and status.
MRP
Performs Redo Apply on a physical standby.
Recovery process state, apply progress and lag metrics.
Standby datafiles
Hold the physical database copy updated by recovery.
Database role/open mode and successful recovery progress.

blocks.label: Architecture checkpoint
blocks.text: For each layer, collect evidence independently. A network or destination error points to transport; a received-but-not-applied sequence points toward apply, recovery, or standby resource constraints.

Before creating the standby, establish the target topology and confirm compatibility. A build that succeeds technically can still be operationally unsafe if naming, storage, redo thread coverage, password files, network routing, or backup retention are not planned.

items: Use a supported and compatible Oracle Database software release and patch level for the intended Data Guard configuration. Check the current Oracle 19c documentation and interoperability rules for the exact RU and platform.
Use ARCHIVELOG mode on the primary. Confirm that archived redo can be retained long enough to cover expected network or standby outages.
Evaluate FORCE LOGGING. It is commonly enabled to prevent unrecoverable direct-path operations from creating gaps in the standby, but assess workload and operational implications before changing it.
Set distinct DB_UNIQUE_NAME values for primary and standby while keeping the intended DB_NAME consistent.
Configure Oracle Net connectivity in both directions as required by the chosen build method and validate service resolution.
Prepare password-file authentication for redo transport and administrative operations. Protect and distribute the file using approved secret-handling procedures.
Plan datafile, tempfile, control-file, online redo and standby redo log locations. Confirm capacity, permissions, ASM disk groups or filesystem mounts.
For RAC, plan redo threads and standby redo log groups for every primary thread.

sections.heading: 4. Build workflow — from primary preparation to managed recovery

blocks.text: There are multiple supported ways to instantiate a physical standby, including RMAN DUPLICATE FOR STANDBY and backup-based workflows. The exact commands depend on storage naming, ASM versus filesystem, Oracle Net aliases, encryption, RAC, and whether Oracle Managed Files are used. Treat this as the sequence and decision checklist, not a copy-and-run script.

items: Capture the primary baseline
Record DB_NAME, DB_UNIQUE_NAME, DBID, role, open mode, ARCHIVELOG, FORCE LOGGING, redo threads, online redo sizes, current archive sequence and database version/RU.
Prepare the standby host
Install compatible Oracle software, apply the approved patch level, create required directories or ASM disk groups, set ownership/permissions, and verify storage capacity.
Configure connectivity and authentication
Create and test the required Oracle Net service aliases. Configure the listener and password file according to the selected deployment method. Do not expose passwords in scripts or shell history.
Prepare standby initialization

Set the standby DB_UNIQUE_NAME and required Data Guard parameters. Plan DB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT / LOG_FILE_NAME_CONVERT only if the storage layout requires them; OMF/ASM designs may use different mapping approaches.
Instantiate the standby

Use a documented RMAN duplicate or backup/restore procedure. Confirm that the standby control file and datafiles correspond to a consistent primary backup and that all required archived redo is available.
Configure redo transport
Configure the primary remote archive destination and standby destination state using the approved parameter strategy. Validate service connectivity and destination errors before relying on transport.
Create standby redo logs

Create SRLs with appropriate sizing and sufficient groups for each redo thread. A common planning rule is at least one more SRL group per thread than the number of online redo log groups for that thread; validate the exact design against Oracle documentation and topology.
Start Redo Apply
Mount the physical standby and start managed recovery using the documented command for the intended real-time or archived-log apply mode. Avoid starting duplicate recovery processes.
Validate end to end
Generate a controlled test transaction in the lab, observe transport and apply, compare thread/sequence progress, inspect Data Guard metrics and alert logs, and document the measured lag.

blocks.label: Production safety
blocks.text: Do not run role transitions, FORCE LOGGING changes, destination changes, RMAN duplicate, or recovery start/stop commands in production merely by copying this lesson. Use an approved change, tested runbook, prechecks, backup/recovery plan and rollback/contingency decision.

sections.heading: 5. Commands and validation — understand the evidence

blocks.text: Confirm database identity and role

SELECT name, db_unique_name, database_role, open_mode, protection_mode
FROM   v$database;

On the primary, expect DATABASE_ROLE to identify PRIMARY. On the standby, expect PHYSICAL STANDBY. The physical standby is normally mounted while Redo Apply is running; Active Data Guard real-time query is a separately licensed capability and changes the open-mode design.
Inspect standby redo log configuration
Check that SRLs exist for the relevant redo threads, have appropriate size, and are not all unavailable or incorrectly configured. In RAC, do not validate only thread 1.
Inspect transport destination health

SELECT dest_id, status, error, destination, target
FROM   v$archive_dest_status
WHERE  status <> 'INACTIVE'
ORDER  BY dest_id;
Review STATUS and ERROR together. A destination marked valid at one point in time is not proof that current redo is arriving. Correlate with alert-log messages and sequence progress.
Inspect Data Guard lag

Interpret lag with TIME_COMPUTED and DATUM_TIME. Stale metrics or a lack of recent redo activity can mislead. Confirm the latest received and applied sequence per thread and investigate the underlying transport/apply layer.

sections.heading: 6. Hands-on lab — isolated two-host or two-instance environment

blocks.text: Goal: create a physical standby for a disposable Oracle 19c primary and prove that a controlled change reaches and is applied on the standby. Use lab-only names, storage and credentials.

items: Record primary DB_NAME, DB_UNIQUE_NAME, DBID, database_role, open_mode and protection mode.
Capture ARCHIVELOG, FORCE LOGGING, online redo log groups and redo thread details.
Confirm standby host storage, Oracle home, listener, service aliases and password-file plan.
Choose RMAN duplicate or backup/restore instantiation and write down the exact release-specific procedure before execution.
Configure and verify standby redo logs for every required thread.
Start Redo Apply and capture the process state.
Generate a small controlled lab transaction and commit it on the primary.
Verify that the corresponding redo is received and applied on the standby.
Capture lag metrics, sequence evidence and alert-log timestamps.
Stop or reset the lab only using the documented lab teardown procedure.

blocks.label: Evidence to retain
blocks.text: Keep the before/after SQL output, RMAN log, alert-log excerpts from both databases, timestamps, DB_UNIQUE_NAME values, thread/sequence observations and a short conclusion. This turns a lab exercise into an auditable DBA runbook.

rows: Remote destination error
Oracle Net, listener, service alias, authentication, firewall, destination parameter.
V$ARCHIVE_DEST_STATUS, alert log, listener log, connectivity tests.
Redo received but apply is behind
MRP state, recovery errors, missing archive sequence, standby I/O or CPU pressure.
V$DATAGUARD_STATS, V$ARCHIVED_LOG, recovery process state, alert log.
Archive gap reported
Missing thread/sequence, archive deletion/retention, network interruption.
Thread and sequence ranges on both sites; archive availability on primary/backup.
RFS not visible
No current redo activity, transport not configured/connected, destination error.
Primary destination status, standby alert log, process state and network evidence.
Apply lag grows under load
Redo generation rate exceeds apply capacity or standby resources are constrained.
Redo MB/s, apply rate, I/O latency, CPU, parallel recovery configuration and waits.

items: Detect and timestamp
Record when the symptom began and whether it is continuous or intermittent.
Separate transport from apply
Determine whether the latest primary redo has arrived at the standby. Do not treat apply lag as proof of a network problem.
Correlate thread and sequence
Compare received and applied sequence progress for every thread. Check for gaps rather than relying on one aggregate lag number.
Collect diagnostic evidence
Review dynamic performance views, Broker status if Broker is used, database alert logs, listener logs and host/network metrics.
Choose the smallest safe correction
Correct the failing layer only after confirming the cause. Preserve logs and avoid destructive archive cleanup or unplanned role transitions.
Validate and document
Prove that transport and apply resumed, lag returned to the expected range, and the incident timeline and root cause are recorded.

sections.heading: 8. Senior DBA design review and knowledge check

blocks.text: Questions to defend in an architecture review

items: What RPO and RTO does the business require, and which protection mode and transport configuration support that target?
What happens if the primary site is lost while the standby has unapplied redo?
How are archive gaps recovered if the primary no longer has the required archived logs?
How do redo generation rate, network bandwidth, standby I/O and apply throughput interact?
How will backups, TDE wallets, password files, patching and monitoring be handled across both sites?
What is the tested procedure for switchover, failover, reinstate and returning to the preferred topology?

blocks.label: Senior DBA perspective
blocks.text: A successful build is not simply “the standby is mounted.” It is a documented and tested service: transport and apply are observable, RPO/RTO are measured, backups are independent, failure decisions are explicit, and recovery has been rehearsed.

questions.q: Which standby process receives redo from the primary?
questions.explanation: RFS (Remote File Server) receives incoming redo on the standby and writes it to the configured redo destination.

questions.q: Which process performs Redo Apply on a physical standby?
questions.explanation: MRP (Managed Recovery Process) applies redo to the physical standby database.

questions.q: A destination is healthy and redo is arriving, but apply lag is increasing. What should you investigate first?
options: Apply/recovery state and standby resource constraints
questions.explanation: Separate transport from apply. Check MRP/recovery errors, gaps, I/O, CPU and apply throughput before making changes.

questions.q: Does a physical standby replace independent backups?
questions.explanation: A standby can replicate logical mistakes or corruption. Independent, tested backups remain essential.

sections.heading: 2. Architecture and internal workflow
sections.content: Use SHOW CONFIGURATION, SHOW DATABASE VERBOSE and VALIDATE commands; investigate warnings rather than suppressing them.\n\nTrace the flow from primary redo generation through transport, standby receipt, storage in standby redo logs, and apply. sections.heading: 3. Administration commands and validation
4. Hands-on lab
sections.content:
Lab objective: reproduce this topic in an isolated Oracle 19c primary/physical-standby environment.

1. Record DB_NAME, DB_UNIQUE_NAME, database_role, open_mode and protection mode on both members.
2. Capture the baseline using the validation queries above.
3. Perform the topic-specific exercise in a disposable lab, following the release-specific Oracle documentation.
4. Capture before/after outputs, alert-log excerpts and timestamps.
5. Confirm transport and apply return to a healthy state.
6. Restore the lab to its baseline or document the resulting topology.

Expected evidence: a reproducible command transcript, observed state change, and post-test validation.

sections.heading: 5. Troubleshooting and production scenarios
sections.content: Use the sequence: Detect → Collect evidence → Separate transport from apply → Identify the failing layer → Apply the smallest safe correction → Validate → Record RCA.\n\nCheck V$DATAGUARD_STATS, V$ARCHIVE_DEST_STATUS, V$ARCHIVED_LOG, standby redo logs, managed recovery processes, Broker output and the database alert log. sections.heading: 6. Senior DBA and architect interview preparation
sections.content:

• What are the prerequisites and failure modes?
• How do you prove it is working rather than merely configured?
• What is the impact on RPO, RTO, availability, performance and licensing?
• What is your safe recovery or rollback path?

Scenario: a standby is behind during a maintenance window. Describe the evidence you collect, the decision criteria, the communication plan and the validation after remediation.
